'''Magdalena Żernicka-Goetz''' (born 30 August 1963)<ref name=whoswho/> {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FMedSci}}<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://zernickagoetzlab.pdn.cam.ac.uk/|title=MZG|website=zernickagoetzlab.pdn.cam.ac.uk|language=en-US|access-date=2017-04-02}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.pdn.cam.ac.uk/directory/magda-zernicka-goetz|title=Magdalena Zernicka-Goetz — Department of Physiology, Development and Neuroscience|last=ri256@cam.ac.uk|website=www.pdn.cam.ac.uk|date=24 September 2015|language=en|access-date=2017-04-02}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sid.cam.ac.uk/aboutus/people/person.html?crsid=mz205|title=College Fellows and Staff - Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge University|website=www.sid.cam.ac.uk|language=en|access-date=2017-04-02}}</ref> is a Polish-British [[developmental biologist]]. She serves as Bren Professor of Biology and [[Biological engineering|Biological Engineering]] at [[California Institute of Technology]] (Caltech).<ref>{{Cite web|title=Magdalena Zernicka-Goetz {{!}} Division of Biology and Biological Engineering|url=http://bbe70.divisions.caltech.edu/people/magdalena-zernicka-goetz?back_url=/people?search=magdalena&category=85&category=&submit=Search#profile-4177b219-tab|access-date=2020-06-18|website=bbe70.divisions.caltech.edu}}</ref><ref name=epmc>{{EuropePMC}}</ref> She was previously Professor of Mammalian Development and Stem Cell Biology in the [[Department of Physiology, Development and Neuroscience, University of Cambridge|Department of Physiology, Development and Neuroscience]] and Fellow of [[Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge]].

In 2020, she was listed by [[Prospect (magazine)|''Prospect'']] as the 10th-greatest thinker for the [[COVID-19]] era, with the magazine writing, "She's been able to grow human embryos in vitro right up to the current 14-day legal limit."<ref>{{Cite magazine|date=2020|title=The world's top 50 thinkers for the Covid-19 age|url=https://www.prospectmagazine.co.uk/content/uploads/2020/09/PWTT20.pdf|access-date=2020-09-08|magazine=Prospect|archive-date=7 September 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200907185002/https://www.prospectmagazine.co.uk/content/uploads/2020/09/PWTT20.pdf}}</ref>

== Education ==
Żernicka-Goetz was born in [[Warsaw]], Poland in 1963.<ref name=whoswho/> She received her Master of Science degree (''summa cum laude'') in developmental biology (1988) and her PhD degree in the developmental biology of mammals (1993) from the [[University of Warsaw]], with one year (1990–91) spent at the [[University of Oxford]]. She carried out her Ph.D. studies with [[Andrzej Tarkowski]] (Warsaw) and Chris Graham (Oxford).<ref name="CV">{{Citation |last=Żernicka-Goetz |first=Magdalena |title=Curriculum Vitae. MAGDALENA ZERNICKA-GOETZ, Ph.D. FMedSci |url=https://mzglab.files.wordpress.com/2021/06/magdalena-zernicka-goetz-cv-june-2021-1.pdf|publication-date=2021}}</ref>

== Career and research ==
After obtaining her Ph.D., Zernicka-Goetz spent two years as a [[postdoctoral]] [[European Molecular Biology Organization]] (EMBO) fellow with [[Martin Evans]] in the [[Wellcome Trust]] / [[Cancer Research UK]] Institute (now the [[Gurdon Institute]]) in Cambridge. In 1997, she started her independent group in the Gurdon Institute where she was a Lister Institute Senior [[Research fellow|Research Fellow]] (1997-2002) and subsequently a Wellcome Trust Senior Research Fellow. In 2007, she was awarded a readership and in 2010 a professorship at the University of Cambridge.{{Citation needed|date=May 2020}}In 2014, she moved her laboratory to the Department of Physiology, Development and Neuroscience of the University of Cambridge. In 2019, the laboratory moved to the California Institute of Technology (Caltech). 

Upon setting up her independent group in 1997, she studied the mechanisms regulating early mammalian development. To do this, she was first to establish [[RNA interference]] in mammalian cells to determine cell fate in the mouse embryos.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Wianny F, Zernicka-Goetz M | title = Specific interference with gene function by double-stranded RNA in early mouse development | journal = Nature Cell Biology | volume = 2 | issue = 2 | pages = 70–5 | date = February 2000 | pmid = 10655585 | doi = 10.1038/35000016 | s2cid = 2568655 }}</ref> At that time, she also began to trace the origins and destinies of cells in the preimplantation mouse embryo that let her to discover that cell fate specification begins earlier than expected,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Piotrowska K, Zernicka-Goetz M | title = Role for sperm in spatial patterning of the early mouse embryo | journal = Nature | volume = 409 | issue = 6819 | pages = 517–21 | date = January 2001 | pmid = 11206548 | doi = 10.1038/35054069 | bibcode = 2001Natur.409..517P | s2cid = 4416599 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | Her recent development of systems permitting both mouse and human embryogenesis during implantation and early post-implantation stages ''in vitro'' allowed her to reveal that mouse and human embryo remodelling at implantation is done autonomously by the embryo. She uncovered the mechanism underlying embryo remodelling between the blastocyst and gastrula stages that has led to a change in the textbook model.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Morris SA, Grewal S, Barrios F, Patankar SN, Strauss B, Buttery L, Alexander M, Shakesheff KM, Zernicka-Goetz M | title = Dynamics of anterior-posterior axis formation in the developing mouse embryo | journal = Nature Communications | volume = 3 | page = 673 | date = February 2012 | pmid = 22334076 | pmc = 3293425 | doi = 10.1038/ncomms1671 | doi-access = free| bibcode = 2012NatCo...3..673M }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Bedzhov I, Zernicka-Goetz M | title = Self-organizing properties of mouse pluripotent cells initiate morphogenesis upon implantation | journal = Cell | volume = 156 | issue = 5 | pages = 1032–44 | date = February 2014 | pmid = 24529478 | pmc = 3991392 | doi = 10.1016/j.cell.2014.01.023 }}</ref> The demonstration of the self-organisation of human embryos developing ''in vitro'' until day 13/14, by Zernicka-Goetz and Ali Brivanlou groups, has provided an unprecedented opportunity to study human development at previously inaccessible and critical stages.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Shahbazi MN, Jedrusik A, Vuoristo S, Recher G, Hupalowska A, Bolton V, Fogarty NM, Campbell A, Devito LG, Ilic D, Khalaf Y, Niakan KK, Fishel S, Zernicka-Goetz M | title = Self-organization of the human embryo in the absence of maternal tissues | journal = Nature Cell Biology | volume = 18 | issue = 6 | pages = 700–8 | date = June 2016 | pmid = 27144686 | pmc = 5049689 | doi = 10.1038/ncb3347 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Deglincerti |first1=Alessia |last2=Croft |first2=Gist F. |last3=Pietila |first3=Lauren N. |last4=Zernicka-Goetz |first4=Magdalena |last5=Siggia |first5=Eric D. |last6=Brivanlou |first6=Ali H. |date=May 2016 |title=Self-organization of the in vitro attached human embryo |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nature17948 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=533 |issue=7602 |pages=251–254 |doi=10.1038/nature17948 |pmid=27144363 |bibcode=2016Natur.533..251D |s2cid=4461915 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This discovery was hailed as the people's choice for the scientific breakthrough of 2016 by Science magazine.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.cam.ac.uk/research/news/cambridge-study-named-as-peoples-choice-for-science-magazines-breakthrough-of-the-year-2016|title=Cambridge study named as People's Choice for Science magazine's 'Breakthrough of the Year 2016'|date=2016-12-22|work=University of Cambridge|access-date=2017-04-02|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/ripples-spacetime-sciences-2016-breakthrough-year|title=Ripples in spacetime: Science's 2016 Breakthrough of the Year|date=2016-12-19|work=Science {{!}} AAAS|access-date=2017-04-02|language=en}}</ref>  The knowledge she gained through her work on how the embryo develops during the blastocyst to gastrula transition, allowed her to mimic these developmental processes with different types of stem cells in vitro. This led her to the pioneering success of constructing embryo-like structures from pluripotent embryonic and multipotent extra-embryonic (trophoblast) stem cells in a 3D scaffold of extra-cellular matrix proteins in vitro.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Harrison SE, Sozen B, Christodoulou N, Kyprianou C, Zernicka-Goetz M | title = Assembly of embryonic and extra-embryonic stem cells to mimic embryogenesis in vitro | journal = Science | volume = 356 | issue = 6334 | article-number = eaal1810 | date = March 2017 | pmid = 28254784 | doi = 10.1126/science.aal1810 | s2cid = 3863929 | url = https://authors.library.caltech.edu/94534/2/Harrison.SM.pdf }}</ref> These "synthetic embryos" recapitulate the natural architecture of the embryo and their patterns of gene expression leading to the specification of the germ layers and germ cells. This system allowed her to identify signalling pathways responsible for morphogenesis of stem cells into embryos. Together these models bring outstanding potential for understanding development and for [[regenerative medicine]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last=Zimmer |first=Carl |date=2023-06-24 |title=Scientists Debut Lab Models of Human Embryos |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/06/24/science/human-embryos-lab-models-fertility.html |access-date=2023-12-16 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> In 2023, her team was among several that reported creating the first human embryo models.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite report |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/biologists-use-human-stem-cells-create-embryo-replicas |title=Biologists create detailed lab replicas of early human embryos |date=2023-06-17 |doi=10.1126/science.adj2826 |language=en|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="theguardian/synthetic-human-embryos-created">{{cite news |last1=Devlin |first1=Hannah |date=14 June 2023 |title=Synthetic human embryos created in groundbreaking advance |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2023/jun/14/synthetic-human-embryos-created-in-groundbreaking-advance |access-date=15 June 2023}}</ref><ref name="bbc/65914934">{{cite news |date=15 June 2023 |title=First synthetic human embryo raises ethical issues |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/health-65914934 |access-date=15 June 2023}}</ref>

Żernicka-Goetz's group have shown that sperm entry induces actomyosin-driven cytoplasmic flows that are predictive of successful development to birth in the mouse. This provides an opportunity to identify quantitatively and non-invasively the healthiest embryos to transfer to would-be-mothers in IVF.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Ajduk A, Ilozue T, Windsor S, Yu Y, Seres KB, Bomphrey RJ, Tom BD, Swann K, Thomas A, Graham C, Zernicka-Goetz M | title = Rhythmic actomyosin-driven contractions induced by sperm entry predict mammalian embryo viability | journal = Nature Communications | volume = 2 | page = 417 | date = August 2011 | pmid = 21829179 | pmc = 3265380 | doi = 10.1038/ncomms1424 | doi-access = free| bibcode = 2011NatCo...2..417A }}</ref>

Stimulated by the finding of placental cells with abnormal chromosome complements (aneuploid cells) in her own pregnancy, she began to study the consequence of aneuploidy upon development in a mouse model. Her lab generated an experimental model to find that aneuploid cells arising during embryogenesis in the mouse embryo become eliminated by [[apoptosis]] in embryonic but not extra-embryonic tissues. This gives insight into why mosaic aneuploidy identified by chorionic-villus-sampling can be tolerated in human pregnancies.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Bolton H, Graham SJ, Van der Aa N, Kumar P, Theunis K, Fernandez Gallardo E, Voet T, Zernicka-Goetz M | title = Mouse model of chromosome mosaicism reveals lineage-specific depletion of aneuploid cells and normal developmental potential | journal = Nature Communications | volume = 7 | article-number = 11165 | date = March 2016 | pmid = 27021558 | pmc = 4820631 | doi = 10.1038/ncomms11165 | doi-access = free| bibcode = 2016NatCo...711165B }}</ref>

The potential impact of Żernicka-Goetz's work is now becoming widely recognised through her public engagement.<ref>{{Citation|last=Stanford|title=Magdalena Zernicka-Goetz - Conception and Early Development|date=2016-06-08|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7cZhuXTvfis|access-date=2017-04-02}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Vogel G | title = Pushing the limit | journal = Science | volume = 354 | issue = 6311 | pages = 404–407 | date = October 2016 | pmid = 27789822 | doi = 10.1126/science.354.6311.404| s2cid = 8343004 }}</ref>

Her book "The Dance of Life" co-authored with [[Roger Highfield]],<ref>The Dance of Life {{ISBN missing}}</ref> describes her scientific and personal journey devoted to understanding the earliest stages of our own life and the critical issue of [[women in science]].

=== Awards and honors ===
Żernicka-Goetz was elected a member of the [[European Molecular Biology Organization]] (EMBO) in 2007,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.embo.org/documents/news/press_releases/2007/new_embo_members_07.pdf|title=EMBO Members elected 2007}}</ref> a [[Fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences]] (FMedSci),<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://acmedsci.ac.uk/fellows/fellows-directory/ordinary-fellows/fellow/Professor-Magdalena-Zernicka-Goetz-0008953|title=Professor Magdalena Zernicka-Goetz {{!}} The Academy of Medical Sciences|website=acmedsci.ac.uk|access-date=2017-04-02}}</ref> 2013, and a foreign member of [[Polish Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 2016. Other awards and honours include:

* 2023 Ogawa-Yamanaka Stem Cell Prize
* 2023 ESHG Lecture Award 
* 2022 [[Society for Developmental Biology]] Edwin G. Conklin Medal<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-01-25 |title=Magdalena Zernicka-Goetz Receives Prestigious Developmental Biology Honors |url=https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/magdalena-zernicka-goetz-receives-prestigious-developmental-biology-honors |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=California Institute of Technology |language=en}}</ref>
* 2022 ''NOMIS Foundation'' 'Distinguished Scientist and Scholar' Awardee<ref>https://nomisfoundation.ch/people/magdalena-zernicka-goetz/</ref>
* Top ten in ''Prospect Magazine's'' 'World's Top 50 Thinkers for the COVID-19 Age'
*''The Times'' 'Science Power List', May 2020<ref>{{Cite news|last=Franklin-Wallis|first=Oliver|date=23 May 2020|title=From pandemics to cancer: the science power list|language=en|work=[[The Times]]|url=https://www.thetimes.com/uk/healthcare/article/from-pandemics-to-cancer-the-science-power-list-d23bb9b2k|access-date=2020-05-26|issn=0140-0460}}</ref>
*International Foundation IVI Award for the Best Basic Research in Reproductive Medicine, 2017<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.ivifoundation.net/en/The-Foundation.aspx | title = The Foundation | last = IVI | first = Fundación | website = www.ivifoundation.net | language=en-GB | access-date = 2017-04-02 }}</ref>
* Foreign Member of Polish Academy of Arts and Sciences, elected 2016
* Winner of the People's Vote for Scientific Breakthrough of the year 2016 by Science magazine
* [[Fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences]] 2013
* [[Anne McLaren]] Memorial Lecture Award, International Society of Differentiation, 2008
* Member of [[European Molecular Biology Organisation]], elected 2007
* Young Investigator Award, EMBO (2001-2004)
* Wellcome Trust Senior Research Fellowship (2002-2008, 2008–2013, 2013–2018)
* Lister Institute of Preventative Medicine Senior Research Fellowship (1997-2002)
* EMBO Long-term Fellowship for post-doctoral studies at the University of Cambridge (1995-1997)
* Best Ph.D. thesis Award, Polish Ministry of Education, 1994{{citation needed|date=January 2023}}
* Promising Young Scientist Prize, [[Foundation for Polish Science]], 1993

==Personal life==
Żernicka-Goetz married [[David Glover (geneticist)|David Glover]] in 2000 and has two children.<ref name=whoswho>{{Who's Who | author=Anon| title=Zernicka-Goetz, Prof. Magdalena | id = U279614 | year = 2017 | doi =10.1093/ww/9780199540884.013.U279614 | edition = online [[Oxford University Press]]|location=Oxford}}</ref>
